entry.title: Hardening TLS on NetScaler VPX, revisited
entry.content:
Every few years I end up back in the NetScaler console, staring at the same cipher-suite dialog and trying to remember which knobs actually matter. This is the note I wish I'd written last time.

The goal is simple: an A+ on SSL Labs, without locking out the two or three clients that still matter to the business. Everything below assumes VPX 14.x with the default front-end vserver.

Start from a known baseline

Before changing anything, capture the current profile. It makes rollback a one-liner and gives you something to diff against later:

show ssl vserver vs_www_443 | grep -i cipher
show ssl profile ns_default_ssl_profile_frontend

If you skip this step you will regret it the first time a partner calls to say their integration stopped working at 3 a.m.

The cipher group I actually ship

After some back-and-forth with SSL Labs I settled on a small, explicit group rather than one of the built-in bundles. TLS 1.3 first, then a short TLS 1.2 tail for legacy callers:

add ssl cipher cg_2026_modern
bind ssl cipher cg_2026_modern -cipherName TLS1.3-AES256-GCM-SHA384 -cipherPriority 1
bind ssl cipher cg_2026_modern -cipherName TLS1.3-AES128-GCM-SHA256 -cipherPriority 2
bind ssl cipher cg_2026_modern -cipherName TLS1.2-ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384 -cipherPriority 3

Bind it to the vserver, re-run SSL Labs, and you should be done. If you aren't, the next section is the usual culprit.

Next post: a ukulele arrangement of Wichita Lineman — because balance.

entry.title: A ukulele arrangement of Wichita Lineman
entry.content:
Jimmy Webb's Wichita Lineman is a three-minute masterclass in longing. The chord changes do most of the work — all I've tried to do is get out of their way.

I've arranged it for a soprano uke in low-G. Standard tuning works, but the low string gives the verses somewhere to sit.

The shape of it

  • Verse: F — C/E — Dm — Bb — F — C — F
  • Refrain: Bb — F — Gm — C — F

Play the verse fingerstyle, thumb on the low string, fingers walking through the top three. When the refrain arrives, let the strum open up — but only just.

Notes

  • The signature line ("and I need you more than want you") sits on the B♭. Hold it a beat longer than feels right.
  • The string-bend that Glen Campbell plays at the end of each verse translates surprisingly well to a pull-off on the A-string, fret 3 → fret 1.
  • Don't try to sing it at Campbell's key. Capo up two frets and give your throat a fighting chance.

I'll post a recording when I'm less embarrassed by mine.

entry.title: PowerShell one-liners I keep reaching for
entry.content:
A small personal cheatsheet — the commands I type two or three times a week and would rather not rediscover every time.

Find which process is holding a port

Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 443 |
  Select-Object LocalAddress, State, OwningProcess,
    @{n="Process";e={(Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess).Name}}

Nicer than netstat -ano | findstr because you get the process name in the same line.

The last thousand events from one log

Get-WinEvent -LogName System -MaxEvents 1000 |
  Where-Object { $_.LevelDisplayName -in 'Error','Warning' } |
  Format-Table TimeCreated, Id, ProviderName, Message -AutoSize

I tend to paste this into a fresh window when a box starts misbehaving — quick situational awareness before I go digging.

Hash a file the same way everywhere

Get-FileHash .\installer.msi -Algorithm SHA256 | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Hash

Pipes nicely into | Set-Clipboard on Windows 11, which is how I paste hashes into change tickets.

None of these are clever. They're just the ones I've given up trying to remember.

entry.title: Recording the uke with a $40 lavalier
entry.content:
I spent a long time convincing myself I needed a large-diaphragm condenser, a proper interface, and an acoustically-treated corner. Then I recorded a passable demo with a Rode smartLav+ clipped to the headstock of my soprano and my phone in aeroplane mode on a book.

Here's what I've learned after twenty or thirty takes that way.

Placement

  • Clip the lav to the headstock, not the body. The headstock is quieter (less boom) and the mic ends up roughly a foot from the soundhole.
  • Angle it across the strings, not towards the soundhole. Pointing straight at the hole exaggerates low-mid honk.
  • Slack the cable. If the cable is taut it transmits finger noise up the fretting hand like a telegraph.

The phone

An iPhone's voice-memo app records 16-bit / 44.1 kHz mono, which is fine. The bigger wins:

  • Turn on aeroplane mode. No notifications, no LTE buzz.
  • Record a ten-second room-tone clip at the start of every session. It makes noise reduction in post much more forgiving.
  • Never let the phone touch the floor — footsteps will end up in the take.

Post

I use Audacity. Two moves cover most of it:

  1. Noise reduction sampled from that room-tone clip (12 dB, sensitivity 6, frequency smoothing 3).
  2. A gentle high-pass at 80 Hz to get rid of the rumble the lav picks up.

That's it. No compression, no EQ beyond the high-pass. A recording made this way won't get you on the radio, but it'll happily sit on a blog post next to the chord chart, and that's what I wanted.
